paragraphs: Image super-resolution models reconstruct higher-resolution images, but compressing their numerical representations can reduce reconstruction quality. Transformer-based models are particularly affected because their internal activations have distributions that are difficult to represent with few bits. This paper introduces 2DQuant, a two-stage method for quantizing an already trained model while retaining more of its accuracy.

The first stage examines weights and activations, whose distributions combine symmetric and asymmetric patterns with long tails. Distribution-Oriented Bound Initialization uses different search strategies to select initial quantization bounds. The second stage, Distillation Quantization Calibration, refines the quantizer parameters by having the compressed model learn from its full-precision counterpart. Together, these stages address both initial numerical range selection and subsequent calibration.

Experiments across bit widths and scaling factors report competitive results from initialization alone and improvements over existing post-training quantization after calibration. At two bits, the reported PSNR gain reaches 4.52 dB on Set5 at twofold enlargement. The abstract also reports 3.60-fold compression and 5.08-fold acceleration, connecting reconstruction improvements with deployment efficiency.
neurips-2024-2dquant-low-bit-post-traini.tldr: 2DQuant combines distribution-aware initialization and teacher-guided calibration to improve low-bit image super-resolution.

paragraphs: One approach to offline reinforcement learning trains a sequence model on previously collected trajectories, then asks it for actions associated with high returns. This paper argues that accurate trajectory modeling is only part of the problem. The model must also answer the probabilistic questions needed to select rewarding actions efficiently and accurately.

Those questions become difficult because both the behavior that collected the data and the environment can be stochastic. Choosing actions therefore requires conditional generation, sometimes with additional constraints. The authors observe that crude approximations to these queries can erode the benefits of expressive sequence models. Their method, Trifle, uses tractable generative models that support exact, efficient probabilistic inference to connect learned trajectories with action selection.

Across nine Gym-MuJoCo benchmarks, Trifle achieves seven state-of-the-art scores and the highest average score against the evaluated baselines. It also substantially improves on prior approaches in stochastic environments and safe reinforcement learning tasks with minimal algorithm changes. These findings support treating inference capability as a central design choice alongside the quality of the sequence model.
neurips-2024-a-tractable-inference-persp.tldr: Trifle improves offline reinforcement learning by making the probabilistic queries behind action selection exact and efficient.

paragraphs: Camera sensors produce different noise patterns, so a denoising model trained on one sensor may transfer poorly to another. Collecting a large training set for each new sensor is time-consuming. This paper develops adaptive domain learning for RAW image denoising, combining existing data from other sensors with a small amount from the target sensor.

The training scheme addresses a specific transfer problem: some source images actually lower target performance when included in fine-tuning. It automatically removes source data that are harmful because of differences between sensor domains. A separate modulation module incorporates sensor type and ISO information, allowing the denoising model to use these characteristics when interpreting its input.

Experiments on public datasets covering smartphone and DSLR cameras show improvements over prior cross-domain denoising methods when little target-sensor data is available. The contribution is therefore both a way to select useful training data and a way to condition processing on sensor information. The findings support adapting existing data selectively instead of assuming that every additional source example will help.
neurips-2024-adaptive-domain-learning-fo.tldr: Adaptive domain learning improves denoising for new camera sensors by filtering harmful source data and using sensor-specific information.

paragraphs: Evaluating a model becomes difficult when available labels cover a biased subset of the population. For example, clinical labels may exist only for patients who received particular examinations. This paper asks how to acquire additional labels efficiently when the evaluation population differs substantially from the existing labeled data.

The authors represent label collection as a sequential decision problem. Its state is a posterior belief about model performance, and each new batch of labels updates that belief. The policy selects batches to reduce uncertainty at the end of the collection process. To optimize this policy, the method differentiates through simulated sequences of decisions, using path-wise gradients instead of the high-variance REINFORCE estimators discussed in the abstract.

The framework can work with different approaches to uncertainty quantification. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show that even planning one step ahead substantially outperforms heuristics inspired by active learning. The result emphasizes that labels useful for estimating a model's performance need to be chosen around that evaluation objective, with attention to how each batch changes subsequent knowledge.
neurips-2024-adaptive-labeling-for-effic.tldr: Planning which labels to collect can reduce uncertainty about model performance more efficiently under severe distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can be vulnerable to attacks that degrade fairness. Earlier fairness attacks described in this paper require changing connections between existing nodes, an ability that may be unavailable in practice. The authors study a different setting in which an attacker introduces new nodes into the graph.

Their method, Node Injection-based Fairness Attack, combines two principles for deciding how to inject nodes: increasing uncertainty and increasing homophily, or connections among similar nodes. It then optimizes the features of the injected nodes to strengthen the fairness attack. This approach shifts the attack mechanism toward additions to the graph, addressing a setting where existing-node connectivity cannot be manipulated as earlier methods require.

Across three real-world datasets, injecting only 1% additional nodes significantly undermines the fairness of mainstream graph neural networks, including models designed to account for fairness. These results show that fairness-aware training did not prevent the tested injection attacks. The practical research implication is that assessing fairness robustness needs to include changes caused by newly introduced graph entities.
neurips-2024-are-your-models-still-fair-.tldr: NIFA shows that injecting a small number of nodes can substantially degrade graph neural network fairness, including in fairness-aware models.

paragraphs: Teaching can improve a human teacher's own understanding by encouraging clearer explanations and more careful reasoning. This paper investigates whether language models can benefit similarly. Its focus is on improving the model doing the teaching, extending the familiar use of a stronger model to train a student.

The authors design three approaches reflecting different levels of involvement with students: observing their feedback, learning from that feedback, and repeating the learning process iteratively. These ideas fit into existing prompting and training pipelines. Some aim to improve answer accuracy without training, while others use fine-tuning to improve the model's underlying capability. The study reports improvements from incorporating these teaching-based procedures.

Teaching materials that students can learn from through in-context examples exhibit clearer and more accurate logic. The authors also find indications that teaching weaker students might improve stronger models, and that multiple students could help more than one student or the teacher alone. These are preliminary findings, suggesting a possible route toward improvement that depends less exclusively on human-produced data or stronger teachers.
neurips-2024-can-llms-learn-by-teaching-.tldr: This preliminary study finds that incorporating student feedback into teaching can improve language-model reasoning.

paragraphs: Backpropagation is widely used to train neural networks, but aspects of its information flow are difficult to reconcile with biological learning. This paper proposes counter-current learning, a framework for assigning credit to network components that takes inspiration from biological systems exchanging signals in opposite directions.

The framework pairs a feedforward network that processes inputs with a feedback network that processes targets. Signals move through these networks in opposite directions, and each network helps guide the other's updates. More informative signals near the bottom of the feedback network guide the top of the feedforward network, with a corresponding influence in the reverse pairing. Learning therefore involves two interacting transformations between inputs and targets.

Experiments with multilayer perceptrons and convolutional networks on five image datasets show performance comparable to other biologically plausible learning algorithms. The authors also demonstrate an autoencoder application, suggesting potential for unsupervised representation learning. The contribution is a proposed learning mechanism with greater biological plausibility and competitive results within that comparison group, rather than evidence that biological brains actually use it.
neurips-2024-counter-current-learning-a-.tldr: Counter-current learning trains interacting input and target networks through opposing signal flows as a biologically inspired credit-assignment mechanism.

paragraphs: Graph Transformers can model relationships between distant nodes, but their memory requirements often grow quadratically with graph size. Sparse variants reduce this burden, although they may still add many connections and leave dense input graphs largely intact. This paper asks whether training can identify a much smaller set of useful connections.

The key observation is that learned attention scores are often similar across networks of different widths. Spexphormer uses this consistency in two stages. It first trains a narrow network on the full augmented graph, then retains active connections to train a wider network on a substantially sparser graph. The inexpensive initial model thus helps determine which connections the larger model should use.

The authors provide theoretical conditions under which a narrow network's attention scores can match those of a wide network, alongside empirical evidence of consistency. On several graph datasets, the resulting method maintains good performance while sharply reducing memory requirements. The theoretical result is conditional, while the experiments support the practical usefulness of transferring connection choices across network widths.
neurips-2024-even-sparser-graph-transfor.tldr: Spexphormer uses a narrow graph Transformer to select sparse connections for a wider model, substantially reducing memory use.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to select an ordered list of approximately the highest-scoring items while preserving differential privacy. There are d candidate items and k positions to fill, so the collection of possible output sequences grows on the order of d to the power k. Working with this enormous collection creates a computational challenge.

Prior work handles the problem through direct sampling and achieves strong empirical accuracy compared with earlier private selection methods. Its time and memory costs scale approximately as d times k, with logarithmic factors suppressed. The new algorithm improves both costs to approximately d plus k squared. This changes how the candidate-set size and requested list length contribute to computational expense.

Experiments show speed improvements of orders of magnitude over that direct-sampling approach while retaining similar empirical accuracy. The result makes the accuracy achieved by joint sequence selection more computationally accessible in the tested settings. Its main contribution is an efficiency improvement in private top-k selection, with observed accuracy preservation rather than a claim of universally better selected outputs.
neurips-2024-faster-differentially-priva.tldr: The proposed private top-k algorithm substantially reduces time and memory costs while maintaining similar empirical selection accuracy.

paragraphs: Low-Rank Adaptation efficiently fine-tunes large models, but the authors identify a diversity problem when applying it to text-to-image diffusion models. Generated images can copy training examples, particularly with stronger adapters or higher adapter ranks trained on small datasets. FouRA addresses this behavior through a different adaptation design.

The method learns its projections in the Fourier domain and chooses adapter rank flexibly based on the input. This combines a change in the space where adaptation is learned with a mechanism that adjusts how much adaptation capacity is used. The authors associate the adaptive rank mechanism with improved generalization and find that the learned frequency-domain projections are decorrelated.

Experiments and analysis report that FouRA resolves the observed copying and distribution-collapse problems while substantially improving image quality. The decorrelated projections also work effectively when multiple adapters are merged. Although motivated by image generation, the method demonstrates benefits on commonsense reasoning and GLUE language benchmarks. Together, these findings connect the adaptation representation and its input-dependent capacity to both generation diversity and broader fine-tuning performance.
neurips-2024-foura-fourier-low-rank-adap.tldr: FouRA uses Fourier-domain projections and input-dependent adapter ranks to improve fine-tuning diversity, quality, and generalization.

paragraphs: Randomness in training produces different optimized neural networks even within a related family of models. This paper studies that variation through input saliency maps, which describe how model outputs respond to changes in their inputs. It treats trained networks as samples from a distribution of functions and compares their behavior point by point.

The authors observe a surprising trend: two independently optimized models tend to have more similar saliency as either model's capacity increases. They propose that variants within an architecture family share aligned population-average saliency directions, and that larger models concentrate more closely around this shared direction. These statements are presented as hypotheses motivated by the observed convergence trend.

To describe the behavior mathematically, the paper introduces semi-parametric models based on the Saw distribution that accommodate the reported observations. Experiments explore implications for applications including black-box attacks and deep ensembles. The contribution is a distributional account of why increasingly capable models may become more alike in their input sensitivities, with the broader explanation remaining a proposed interpretation of the evidence.
neurips-2024-great-minds-think-alike-the.tldr: The paper observes increasing agreement in input saliency as model capacity grows and proposes a distributional explanation.

paragraphs: Annotating three-dimensional medical images is expensive, especially when expert judgment is required. Active learning aims to reduce that cost by selecting which examples to annotate. This paper focuses on choosing individual slices for 3D segmentation, an approach that can reduce annotation requirements compared with selecting entire volumes.

The proposed method improves the metric used by Coreset selection to compare candidate samples. It combines contrastive learning with groupings inherent in medical imaging so that distances emphasize differences relevant to training a segmentation model. The idea is to make the selection process sensitive to useful distinctions between slices. The method is also evaluated with weak annotations, bringing selective labeling together with less extensive supervision.

Across four medical and non-medical datasets, the approach outperforms existing active learning methods under both weak and full annotation settings. Its strong results at small annotation budgets are especially relevant to costly medical labeling. The findings support learning a task-relevant comparison metric as part of sample selection, rather than treating the representation used to choose examples as a fixed detail.
neurips-2024-integrating-deep-metric-lea.tldr: A learned similarity metric improves slice selection for 3D segmentation, yielding stronger results with limited weak or full annotations.

paragraphs: Large gradient-descent steps can produce an initial period of oscillating training loss followed by steady decreases. This paper analyzes that transition for two-layer networks satisfying a near-homogeneity condition and trained with logistic loss. It seeks to explain when the apparently unstable early behavior gives way to more orderly progress.

The analysis shows that the second phase starts once empirical risk falls below a threshold that depends on the step size. During this phase, the normalized margin grows nearly monotonically, revealing an implicit preference in how gradient descent shapes the predictor. Under the additional assumptions of linearly separable data and an activation derivative bounded away from zero, decreasing average risk ensures that the first phase ends after finitely many steps.

The authors also show that an appropriately large step size, allowing this phase transition, can optimize more efficiently than gradient descent constrained to decrease risk monotonically. The analysis covers networks of any width within its assumptions. The result gives a conditional mathematical explanation for why temporary loss oscillation can accompany faster optimization and improving classification margins.
neurips-2024-large-stepsize-gradient-des.tldr: Under stated network and data conditions, large gradient steps can transition from oscillating loss to efficient optimization with improving margins.

paragraphs: Assistive agents are often designed to infer a person's intention and then help achieve it. That inference can be difficult in high-dimensional environments. This paper instead builds on empowerment: assistance aims to increase how much influence the person's actions have over environmental outcomes, giving them greater control and helping them complete tasks in fewer steps.

The technical contribution uses contrastive successor representations to make this approach scalable. These representations support both estimating an empowerment-related quantity and optimizing it. The authors formally establish that the estimated quantity corresponds to a notion of empowerment similar to the one studied in earlier work. This provides a mathematical connection between the learned representation and the assistance objective.

Experiments show improvements over prior methods on synthetic benchmarks and demonstrate scaling to the cooperative game Overcooked. The results support representation learning as a practical route to empowerment-based assistance in more complex settings. The approach's defining choice is to make human actions more effective without first requiring an inferred reward function that specifies the human's intended goal.
neurips-2024-learning-to-assist-humans-w.tldr: Contrastive successor representations help assistive agents increase human control without first inferring human rewards.

paragraphs: Anomaly detection benefits from understanding both nearby image details and relationships across an entire image. Convolutional networks struggle with long-range dependencies, while Transformer attention carries quadratic computational costs. This paper introduces MambaAD to use Mamba's long-range modeling and linear efficiency for multi-class unsupervised anomaly detection.

The architecture combines a pretrained encoder with a Mamba decoder containing locality-enhanced state-space modules at multiple scales. These modules pair hybrid state-space blocks with convolutions using multiple kernel sizes, bringing global and local information together. The hybrid blocks turn feature maps into sequences using five scanning methods and eight directions, strengthening connections across spatial locations through the state-space model.

The authors find that Hilbert scanning and processing in eight directions significantly improve feature-sequence modeling. Across six anomaly-detection datasets and seven evaluation metrics, MambaAD achieves state-of-the-art performance. The findings support the combined architectural design: efficient sequence modeling provides broad context, while convolutional operations and scan choices help preserve the spatial information needed to identify anomalies.
neurips-2024-mambaad-exploring-state-spa.tldr: MambaAD combines state-space modeling, multidirectional scanning, and local convolutions for strong unsupervised anomaly detection.

paragraphs: Several model families seek to replace conventional softmax attention with computations that scale linearly. This paper studies how to design such replacements by asking what makes a good linear approximation to the softmax attention map. It first expresses existing linear Transformers, state-space models, and linear recurrent networks within a common linear-attention formulation.

Within that theoretical perspective, the authors identify three design conditions: dynamic memory ability, static approximation ability, and approximation using the least parameters. These conditions bring memory behavior, approximation capability, and parameter economy into the same analysis. The paper finds that the existing linear models it considers do not meet all three, and proposes Meta Linear Attention, or MetaLA, to satisfy them.

Experiments cover associative recall, language modeling, image classification, and the Long-Range Arena benchmark. MetaLA is more effective than existing linear models in these evaluations. The contribution links a unified theoretical account with an architecture designed around its criteria. Its optimality framing concerns those approximation conditions, while the empirical findings demonstrate effectiveness across the reported tasks.
neurips-2024-metala-unified-optimal-line.tldr: MetaLA unifies linear attention designs and satisfies three proposed criteria for approximating softmax attention efficiently.

paragraphs: Image steganography hides a message inside an image, making the choice of that image an important part of the task. Traditional cover selection searches through images using perceptual or complexity measurements. The difficulty is that an image scoring well on those measurements may not actually be well suited to concealing and recovering a message.

This paper replaces exhaustive cover searching with optimization in the latent space of a pretrained generative model. The latent space provides a way to search among images represented by the generator and identify suitable covers. This makes the generative model part of the cover-selection process, addressing the uncertain relationship between conventional selection measurements and actual hiding effectiveness.

The authors report significant advantages in message recovery and image quality. They also analyze the generated covers from an information-theoretic perspective and find that message hiding occurs mainly in low-variance pixels. They relate this pattern to waterfilling in parallel Gaussian channels. This observation offers an interpretation of where the message is carried in the generated covers, alongside the empirical performance findings.
neurips-2024-neural-cover-selection-for-.tldr: Optimizing within a pretrained generator's latent space finds cover images with improved message recovery and image quality.

paragraphs: Gradual stacking trains a model by increasing its depth in stages, using previously trained layers to initialize the larger model. This paper investigates how that training procedure influences what a language model learns, beyond its computational savings. The authors introduce MIDAS, a stacking variant that speeds up training by up to 40%.

MIDAS also improves downstream performance, especially on reasoning-related tasks such as reading comprehension and mathematics. These improvements occur even when perplexity is similar to or slightly worse than conventional training. To examine the effect more directly, the authors create simple synthetic reasoning primitives and find substantial benefits from stacking both before and after fine-tuning.

The training-efficiency and reasoning findings hold in the reported evaluations at one, two, and eight billion parameters. They suggest that how depth is introduced during training can influence reasoning performance in ways not fully reflected by perplexity. The authors explore a connection to looped models as a possible explanation and provide supporting empirical analysis, while presenting that underlying explanation as a conjecture.
neurips-2024-on-the-inductive-bias-of-st.tldr: MIDAS gradually stacks model layers to accelerate training and empirically improve reasoning despite similar or slightly worse perplexity.

paragraphs: Control as inference expresses action selection through a probabilistic inference problem. This paper extends that perspective to risk-sensitive control using variational inference based on Rényi divergence. The resulting framework connects risk sensitivity with a log-probability-regularized control objective that extends maximum-entropy control.

The authors prove that the optimal risk-sensitive policy can be found through a soft Bellman equation. This establishes relationships among the new framework, maximum-entropy control, the optimal posterior in control as inference, and linearly solvable control. They also derive risk-sensitive versions of policy-gradient and soft actor-critic methods, translating the theoretical formulation into reinforcement-learning approaches.

As the risk-sensitivity parameter approaches zero, the formulation recovers risk-neutral control as inference and reinforcement learning. This limiting relationship makes the framework a common description of both settings. The paper additionally develops a distinct extension of maximum-entropy control using Rényi entropy regularization. Despite their different derivations, the two extensions yield optimal policies with the same structure, revealing a shared mathematical organization across the proposed risk-sensitive formulations.
neurips-2024-risk-sensitive-control-as-i.tldr: Rényi-divergence inference provides a unified formulation of risk-sensitive control and corresponding reinforcement-learning methods.

paragraphs: This paper develops a theoretical framework for reinforcement learning when both states and actions vary continuously. It uses that framework to prove fast convergence rates in offline learning from existing data and online learning through interaction. The analysis centers on stability: how changes in learned quantities affect the objects used to describe and improve behavior.

Two stability properties carry the argument. One concerns the effect of changes in value functions or policies on the Bellman operator, which organizes value updates. The other concerns occupation measures, which describe where a policy spends its time in the environment. Studying both connects local changes in learning with their consequences for the distribution of experience.

The authors argue that these properties hold in many continuous-state, continuous-action Markov decision processes. They also use the framework to offer new perspectives on pessimism in offline learning and optimism in online learning. The contribution is a stability-based explanation of fast learning under the analyzed conditions, giving these two settings a related mathematical treatment.
neurips-2024-taming-data-hungry-reinforc.tldr: A stability-based framework proves fast reinforcement-learning convergence rates in continuous state and action spaces.

paragraphs: This paper studies how policy-network parameters move during deep reinforcement learning. In experiments with TD3 and RAD, the authors find that activity is highly uneven: learning progresses consistently along only a few major parameter directions, while smaller directions exhibit substantial detours and oscillation-like behavior.

A temporal singular value decomposition of the training path separates major directions from minor ones. Directions associated with large singular values capture dominant movement, while those associated with small values capture less substantial changes. Based on this analysis, Policy Path Trimming and Boosting cancels updates along minor directions and encourages movement along major directions. The method turns observed structure in the history of parameter updates into a modification of subsequent learning.

Experiments report better scores and efficiency for TD3, RAD, and DoubleDQN on MuJoCo, DeepMind Control Suite, and MinAtar tasks, respectively. These findings support using the geometry of the policy's evolving parameters to improve existing algorithms. The method is presented as a general plug-in, with its demonstrated benefits grounded in those evaluated agents and environments.
neurips-2024-the-ladder-in-chaos-improvi.tldr: Policy Path Trimming and Boosting improves tested reinforcement-learning agents by suppressing minor update directions and strengthening major ones.

paragraphs: Learned regularizers help solve inference and inverse problems by assigning lower penalties to plausible data and higher penalties to implausible data. Critic-based training can learn these penalties from measurements and ground-truth distributions, but their resulting structure is poorly understood. This paper studies that structure through a geometric family of regularizers.

The family consists of gauges, also called Minkowski functionals, of star-shaped bodies. It includes regularizers used in practice and shares properties with neural-network parameterizations. The authors examine critic losses derived from variational formulations of statistical distances. Using star geometry and dual Brunn-Minkowski theory, they interpret these losses as geometric quantities called dual mixed volumes that depend on the data distributions.

This interpretation yields exact formulas for optimal regularizers in certain cases. The paper also identifies neural-network architectures that produce star-body gauges and examines when these regularizers have favorable optimization properties. Its contribution is a mathematical bridge between training distributions, critic objectives, and regularizer geometry, with exact solutions established for specific cases within the studied family.
neurips-2024-the-star-geometry-of-critic.tldr: Star geometry explains the structure of a family of critic-trained regularizers and yields exact optima in certain cases.

paragraphs: AI workflows can contain prompts, code, and other components that cannot be optimized through ordinary differentiation. Their feedback may also consist of console messages or user responses instead of a single numerical score. This paper studies how generative models can iteratively update such workflows using both feedback and information about their execution.

The authors formalize Optimization with Trace Oracle, where an optimizer receives an execution trace alongside feedback on the output. The trace helps relate that feedback to the computations and parameters that produced the result. Their Python library, Trace, expresses workflow optimization in this form using PyTorch-like syntax. They then build OptoPrime, a general optimizer that uses a language model to propose updates.

Experiments demonstrate applications including numerical optimization, prompt improvement, hyperparameter tuning, robot-controller design, and code debugging. OptoPrime is often competitive with specialized optimizers in these domains. The central contribution is the use of execution traces as structured optimization information, playing a role analogous to gradients without requiring the workflow itself to be differentiable.
neurips-2024-trace-is-the-next-autodiff-.tldr: Trace uses workflow execution records and rich feedback to support language-model-driven optimization of diverse computational systems.

paragraphs: Adaptive randomized experiments revise treatment allocation as data arrive, but clinically important outcomes may take time to observe. Missing those outcomes during allocation can reduce the efficiency of treatment-effect estimation. This paper incorporates immediately available surrogate outcomes that predict or correlate with the delayed primary outcome.

The proposed design uses surrogate information to guide adaptive allocations while primary outcomes remain incomplete. It accommodates delays that depend on treatment arm and covariates without imposing a parametric distribution on outcomes. Its objective is efficient estimation of the average treatment effect on the primary outcome, so the earlier measurements serve as supporting information for that target.

The authors derive a semiparametric efficiency bound, characterizing the attainable estimation precision in the studied setting. They show that their estimator reaches this bound and is asymptotically normal. Theoretical comparisons and a synthetic HIV study show greater efficiency than a design that excludes surrogate information. The contribution connects an operational allocation strategy with formal estimation guarantees when the outcomes of greatest interest arrive late.
neurips-2024-using-surrogates-in-covaria.tldr: Immediately observed surrogates improve adaptive treatment allocation and efficient estimation when primary outcomes are delayed.

paragraphs: Sampling from distributions with separated modes can be difficult because movement between regions is obstructed by barriers. This paper studies sampling using only queries to an unnormalized density. It introduces Denoising Diffusion Monte Carlo, a framework that simulates a denoising diffusion process while estimating its score function through Monte Carlo sampling.

The initial framework assumes access to samples needed by the score estimator. The authors implement that sampling component with rejection sampling, producing a concrete algorithm called Zeroth-Order Diffusion Monte Carlo. They establish a general performance guarantee without requiring the target to be log-concave or to satisfy an isoperimetric inequality, broadening the distributional setting covered by the analysis.

For the concrete algorithm, the dependence on desired accuracy is inverse polynomial, although the method still suffers from the curse of dimensionality. Its favorable performance is therefore emphasized for low-dimensional distributions, where it exceeds recent comparison samplers. Experiments also show insensitivity to increasing barriers between modes and discontinuities in non-convex potentials, supporting its usefulness for difficult distribution shapes in that setting.
neurips-2024-zeroth-order-sampling-metho.tldr: ZOD-MC uses density queries and denoising diffusion to sample difficult low-dimensional distributions, while retaining unfavorable dimensional scaling.
